case_study_insert.main_stem: Grange Lane Bricks (GLB) is a public limited company in the construction materials and recycled bricks sector, employing a workforce of 74. Founded in 1998 by Aoife Grange, the business supplies bricks to housebuilders and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GLB plans to invest $880,000 in a recycled-content brick kiln with waste-heat recovery, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and a $380,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and produces 110,000 units of brick a year. GLB faces two operational problems: kiln temperature variation is raising the defect rate, and off-spec rejection is wasting output.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The recycled-content kiln produced 27,500 bricks last quarter with a defect rate of 4.2%, down from 6.8% a year ago. Off-spec rejection wasted 7.4% of output, against a 5% target. Customer complaints from housebuilders fell from 52 to 31 per month. Average delivery is 3.8 days. A survey of 700 housebuilders found that 63% would pay up to $0.35 more per brick for recycled-content products, and 49% check environmental credentials when tendering. A maintenance audit shows 18 of 74 workers have not completed on-the-job training on the new kiln controls; off-the-job courses at the technical centre cost $910 per worker.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Grange Lane Bricks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, raising servicing costs on the $500,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.10 to $14.03 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Clay, recycled aggregate and natural-gas energy costs rose 13.2% year-on-year, while new housing starts fell 2.3% over the same period.

questions.question_text: GLB plans to fund part of its recycled-content kiln with a share issue rather than the $500,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for GLB of using the $380,000 share issue instead of the loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $380,000 raised by the share issue does not require interest or capital repayment, so GLB avoids adding to the interest payable that already rose to $30,000 while carrying a $500,000 bank loan. The saving helps cover fixed costs of $300,000 a year and protects the $6.00 contribution on each brick as clay and energy costs rise 13.2%, allowing the $10.00 price to hold for housebuilders.

Point 2: Equity has no fixed maturity and no security over the kiln, so the $880,000 waste-heat recovery plant cannot be at risk of repossession if the 4.2% defect rate persists or housing starts fall 2.3%. As a public limited company, GLB can also reach a wide pool of investors without surrendering control to a single lender, keeping founder Aoife Grange's strategy intact. The new shareholders share the risk of the recycled-content venture, and the capital strengthens the balance sheet for future borrowing while the 110,000-unit output is established.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to GLB's financing, costs and ownership.

questions.question_text: GLB is promoting its recycled-content bricks to housebuilders. Consider advertising in construction trade journals, sponsoring a housebuilders' association award, or a targeted email and digital campaign. Which should GLB choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Construction trade journal advertising: A trade journal reaches housebuilders and can carry technical data on recycled-content bricks and waste-heat recovery, relevant to the 49% who check environmental credentials when tendering. It lends credibility to a public company. However, full-page advertising is costly for a business with a $500,000 loan, much of the readership is outside GLB's regional market, and print cannot demonstrate brick quality or respond quickly to the 4.2% defect rate concerns.

Housebuilders' association award sponsorship: Sponsoring an award builds prestige and puts GLB in front of senior buyers at one event, supporting the 63% who would pay $0.35 more and the 49% checking credentials. It is a strong relationship-building tool. Its limits are a narrow audience confined to attendees, high sponsorship fees, and the fact that one award cannot by itself secure orders for the 110,000 bricks the kiln produces.

Targeted email and digital campaign: Emails and digital ads can be aimed at regional housebuilders and procurement managers, showing the $0.35 premium message and the 3.8-day delivery record with measurable responses. It is cheap per contact, fast to adjust if kiln defects need explaining, and can be segmented by the 49% who care about credentials. It depends on accurate contact data and sustained follow-up to convert interest into tenders.

Recommendation: GLB should choose the targeted email and digital campaign. It reaches the exact 700-housebuilder survey audience at low cost, can be measured against orders, and scales better than a single award ceremony. The award is rejected as narrow and expensive; trade journals are rejected as costly and untargeted. GLB can enter the awards later as low-cost recognition once the digital campaign has won tenders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to GLB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GLB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GLB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade journals and the award are rejected.

questions.question_text: GLB uses autocratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, and kiln variation is raising the defect rate to 4.2%. Explain two benefits for GLB of this approach in responding to the problem.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership allows founder Aoife Grange to take a quick, decisive response when kiln temperature variation pushes the defect rate to 4.2% and 7.4% of output is rejected. With a clear chain of command in the hierarchy, settings can be standardised and instructions issued immediately across the 74 workers, limiting off-spec production faster than slow consultation and protecting the 110,000-unit output needed to service the $500,000 loan.

Point 2: Clear direction fixes responsibility for the new recycled-content kiln and the $880,000 waste-heat recovery investment, so targets for the 3.8-day delivery and the 5% waste goal are unambiguous. In a large workforce of 74, a hierarchical structure also controls span of command, which helps coordinate the 18 workers still without on-the-job training on the kiln controls and reduces the risk that inconsistent operating habits push complaints back toward the earlier level of 52 per month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GLB's defect rate, scale and kiln investment.

questions.question_text: GLB must train 18 of its 74 workers on the new kiln controls. Consider on-the-job training at the plant or off-the-job courses at the technical centre at $910 per worker. Which should GLB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the kiln teaches the 18 workers the exact control settings behind the recycled-content process, at no course fee, while keeping the 27,500 bricks per quarter flowing. Experienced operators can show how to bring the 4.2% defect rate down and cut the 7.4% rejection rate, and the method suits GLB's direct hierarchy. The drawbacks are that trainers lose production time, mistakes can be copied, and no certificate is issued, which may matter to the 49% of housebuilders checking credentials.

Off-the-job training: The technical centre course at $910 per worker costs $16,380 for all 18 (18 × $910), affordable against the $880,000 kiln, and gives structured teaching plus a recognised qualification that supports GLB's environmental claims. However, 18 of 74 workers are away from the plant during the course, risking the 3.8-day delivery record, and the generic syllabus may not match GLB's exact kiln, so on-site follow-up would be needed.

Decision: GLB should prioritise on-the-job training, adding short certified modules later. It is cheaper, specific to the kiln controls and avoids losing output while the 4.2% defect rate is being tackled; full off-the-job training alone is rejected because withdrawing 18 workers and spending $16,380 would disrupt the 110,000-unit schedule and still leave plant-specific settings to be learned on site.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GLB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of GLB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of GLB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and kiln relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GLB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($10.00 − $4.00) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.00 − $4.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GLB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 50,000 units against output of 110,000 units gives a margin of safety of 60,000 units (110,000 − 50,000), showing how far housing demand could fall before the kiln stops covering $300,000 of fixed costs.
2. Contribution of $6.00 a unit lets managers evaluate the $0.35 premium: if accepted it raises contribution to $6.35, but if housing starts fall 2.3% the 50,000-unit threshold still has to be met, guiding price and tender decisions.
3. The figures set the volume needed to service the $500,000 loan and the $880,000 kiln, informing how much clay and recycled aggregate to order.
4. Unit cost data ($300,000 ÷ 110,000 units + $4.00 = $6.73 a unit) permits quarterly benchmarking, exposing the 7.4% rejection rate and 4.2% defects so management can act on the 13.2% rise in energy and material costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 60,000 units against 110,000-unit output; testing the $0.35 premium against $300,000 fixed costs; loan and $880,000 kiln volume planning; and unit-cost benchmarking at $6.73 to cut rejection.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GLB's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $420,000 on revenue of $1,050,000 gives 420 ÷ 1,050 = 0.400; 2025 gross profit of $540,000 on $1,200,000 gives 540 ÷ 1,200 = 0.450. Operating profit of $126,000 ÷ $1,050,000 = 0.120 and $180,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 0.150. Returns on capital employed of $1,050,000 and $1,200,000 are 126 ÷ 1,050 = 0.120 and 180 ÷ 1,200 = 0.150.

Evaluation: All three measures moved up. The 40.0% to 45.0% rise in the first margin follows revenue growth of $150,000 while cost of sales rose only $30,000, so the extra recycled-content brick sales were earned with comparatively little extra input cost. The 12.0% to 15.0% rise in operating profitability shows the $300,000 fixed costs were absorbed more effectively at 110,000 units, and the 12.0% to 15.0% return on capital shows the new kiln is already contributing. Against this, interest payable rose from $24,000 to $30,000 as the $500,000 loan took effect, and a 13.2% rise in clay, aggregate and gas costs plus a 2.3% fall in housing starts could reverse these gains next year. The 7.4% rejection rate also represents avoidable cost.

Conclusion: GLB's performance has improved. Stronger revenue, a smaller rise in cost of sales and higher operating profit lift both margins and the return on capital. The principal risks are rising interest and input costs together with weaker housing demand, so management should watch them closely, but on the 2024–2025 evidence the improvement is clear.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GLB of producing recycled-content bricks with waste-heat recovery.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled-content bricks with waste-heat recovery support the survey finding that 63% of the 700 housebuilders questioned would pay up to $0.35 more, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit while clay, aggregate and gas costs rise 13.2%. The message also reaches the 49% who check environmental credentials when tendering, supporting the $880,000 kiln and the 110,000-unit output supplied at the $10.00 price.

Disadvantage: Recycled content can vary, which may worsen the current 4.2% defect rate and the 7.4% off-spec rejection rate as the kiln is tuned, pushing up the $4.00 variable cost per unit. Installing and maintaining waste-heat recovery also adds cost and technical complexity, so unless the $0.35 premium is won across tenders, margins will be squeezed while housing starts fell 2.3% and the 3.8-day delivery promise must be kept.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GLB's survey data, costs and kiln quality.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in clay, recycled aggregate and energy costs will affect GLB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If the $500,000 ten-year bank loan carries a variable rate, a 0.75 percentage point increase adds 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year. This is modest against fixed costs of $300,000 and could be removed by fixing the rate, while the $380,000 share issue reduces the need for further debt. A higher rate could nevertheless weaken housebuilder demand at a time when housing starts already fell 2.3%.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.03 an hour): GLB has a workforce of 74 in kiln operations and packing, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert supplies neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 110,000 units ÷ 74 workers ≈ 1,486 bricks per worker. The rise is sustainable only if that output holds and the 4.2% defect rate is reduced, otherwise unit labour costs erode the $6.00 contribution.

Clay, aggregate and energy costs (13.2%): These are the core material and fuel inputs of brick making. The $4.00 variable cost is not broken down, so only a labelled upper bound is possible: if all of it rose 13.2%, that adds 0.132 × $4.00 = $0.53 per brick (rounded); over 110,000 units that is $58,300 a year (110,000 × $0.53). Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution from $6.00 toward about $5.47, and the $0.35 premium available to 63% of builders covers only part of it.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in clay, recycled aggregate and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every brick, directly erodes the contribution that services the $500,000 loan and justifies the $880,000 kiln, and cannot be neutralised by a refinancing decision. The interest rise is quantifiably small at $3,750 and can be fixed, while the wage effect depends on hours not given and can be offset by productivity, so both are subordinate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to GLB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GLB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GLB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
